arguments.heading: Argument analysis: March 25, 2026 session
paragraphs: The Court heard one argument session in this case on March 25, 2026. The main legal question asked whether to adopt a bright-line rule: workers are in interstate commerce only if they cross state lines or interact with vehicles that cross. Flowers Foods endorsed that rule and said a yes-or-no answer would dispose of the case. Brock's side agreed to resolve only the bright-line rule and assumed other issues were off the table here.

Flowers Foods argued that the exemption is limited to workers directly and actively performing cross-border transportation. It said Brock only performs intrastate last-leg work and is not exempt. It described transportation as bookended by loading and unloading on a cross-border vehicle. It said interaction with the vehicle is often relevant, but crossing a border is not strictly required. It also assumed a last-mile framing and did not press title or contract issues.

Brock's side argued that the exemption covers drivers transporting goods on the last leg of an interstate journey. It said personal border crossing or vehicle interaction should not matter. It called the vehicle-interaction requirement atextual and arbitrary. Brock's advocate accepted the phrase intrastate leg of an interstate journey and relied on Supreme Court cases she said reflect the contemporaneous meaning of engaged in commerce.

The justices tested both sides' assumptions. They asked what the final destination of the bread is and what the final destination in this case is. Brock's side answered that the retail stores, Flowers's customers, are the final destination. A justice also questioned splitting workers on an interstate shipment into different categories. The record does not show a holding or vote on any of these questions.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: Flowers Foods makes and delivers bread. Angelo Brock worked as a driver for it. The fight is over a federal labor law exemption. Some transportation workers are exempt from that law's wage rules. The question is whether Brock's work counts as interstate commerce, which would decide whether the exemption applies to him.

The Court was asked to adopt a bright-line rule. Under that rule, workers are in interstate commerce only if they cross state lines themselves, or interact with vehicles that do. That is the core legal question in this case.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The case is Flowers Foods, Inc., et al. v. Angelo Brock, No. 24-935. The Supreme Court heard oral argument in it on March 25, 2026. Traci L. Lovitt argued for Flowers Foods. Jennifer D. Bennett argued for Brock.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Flowers Foods wants a clear rule. It says the exemption covers only workers who directly and actively perform cross-border transportation work. Brock only did intrastate last-leg work, so it says he is not exempt.

Brock's side wants the exemption to cover drivers on the last leg of an interstate journey. It says it does not matter whether the driver personally crossed a border or touched a vehicle that did. It calls the vehicle-interaction requirement atextual and arbitrary.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Flowers Foods endorsed the bright-line rule. It said a yes-or-no answer would dispose of the case. It also described transportation as bookended by loading and unloading on a cross-border vehicle. It said the focus is the class's cross-border transportation work. Interaction with the vehicle is often relevant, but crossing a border is not strictly required.

Flowers Foods also made an assumption for this case. It assumed a last-mile framing and did not press title or contract issues here. It said only Driver 2 is exempt, and that transportation continues until unloading.

Brock's side agreed to resolve only the bright-line rule. It conceded or assumed other issues for this argument. Brock's advocate also accepted the phrase intrastate leg of an interstate journey. She agreed that certain Supreme Court cases reflect the contemporaneous meaning of engaged in commerce, and confirmed her reliance on those cases.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: The justices tested the parties' assumptions. One asked what the final destination of the bread is. Another asked what the final destination in this case is. Brock's side answered that the retail stores, Flowers's customers, are the final destination on this journey.

A justice also raised a concern about splitting workers on an interstate shipment into different categories. That concern probes whether the bright-line rule can cleanly sort workers on one shipment. The record does not show a holding or vote on any of these questions.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: This case matters for delivery workers and companies. A bright-line rule would make it easy to tell who is exempt. A journey-based approach would look at where a shipment starts and ends. The choice affects wages for drivers on the last leg of long trips.
